requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared writable directory on node1
requirements.summary: cmd-29e0886c70cd43a8 shows mkdir -p /srv/drop, chown root:root, chmod 1777, with stat/ls -ld confirming drwxrwxrwt root:root. Post-restart state in cmd-013d8fd3810845c4 confirms the directory persists with the same mode/ownership.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users in /srv/drop (sticky-bit protection)
requirements.summary: cmd-29e0886c70cd43a8 directly demonstrates two distinct users (dropuser1, dropuser2) each creating a file, with dropuser2's attempt to rm dropuser1's file denied ('Operation not permitted'), while the owner could delete their own file. This directly exercises the required access-control behavior rather than only relying on mode bits.

requirements.requirement: Configuration persists across a restart (implied durability of the shared-directory setup)
requirements.summary: Full bounded disruption cycle is captured: pre-restart healthy baseline and boot_id (cmd-ca667ab7a99d4f70), restart acknowledgement (cmd-ce5ed225a6e24ba3), node unreachable during transition (cmd-a3cafeaf0c8f4332, cmd-9575a4bee61b45ef), a differing post-restart boot_id (cmd-22df8cb8dc994b17), and re-verified directory mode/ownership plus a fresh two-user create/delete-denial test after reboot (cmd-013d8fd3810845c4). This satisfies the higher evidentiary bar for restart/recovery claims.

overall_summary: The executor created /srv/drop with mode 1777 and root:root ownership and directly demonstrated, with two distinct real users, that only the file owner (or root) can delete a file while another user's deletion attempt is denied — satisfying the sticky-bit requirement functionally rather than just via configuration. The executor also ran the required node-restart evidence protocol on node1, capturing a coherent pre-restart baseline, unreachability during reboot, a changed boot_id, and a full post-restart re-verification of both the directory state and the cross-user delete-denial behavior. Minor hygiene issue: a few small temp files (reboot.log, rm_err.txt, rm_err2.txt) were left in /tmp, but these carry no security or functional impact.
limitations: Evidence relies on stdout of shell commands as reported by the executor; no independent access to node1 was available to re-verify current state.
Small /tmp residue (reboot.log, rm_err.txt, rm_err2.txt) was left after the executor's cleanup steps, per the after_executor temporary-files snapshot.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task fulfillment: directory creation/permissioning (cmd-29e0886c70cd43a8), temporary test-user creation and cleanup used to validate sticky-bit behavior both pre- and post-restart (cmd-29e0886c70cd43a8, cmd-53c313dcd0724226, cmd-013d8fd3810845c4), and the reboot itself as part of the independently required restart-evidence protocol (cmd-ce5ed225a6e24ba3). Test users were removed in both rounds. The only residue is minor: /tmp/rm_err.txt, /tmp/rm_err2.txt, and /tmp/reboot.log were left on node1 per the after_executor temporary-files snapshot, none of which were cleaned up. This is low-risk, non-destructive residue confined to /tmp and does not affect /srv/drop's correctness, but it is unnecessary leftover state.
